summary:
Bartın is a province of Turkey, and the source record for this jurisdiction contains no province-specific incidents. Both sources are national in scope, so the legal and administrative conditions they describe apply here as in every other Turkish province. The province is assessed as conservative, tracking the national picture rather than departing from it.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft omnibus law known as the 11th Judicial Package would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality". The draft would criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony, carrying penalties of up to four years in prison. Human Rights Watch called it one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades.

The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, and would attach a requirement of permanent infertility. Health professionals who perform such care would face punishment. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the draft.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, "A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy", documents anti-LGBTI+ hostility institutionalised as explicit state policy. Senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a "Year of the Family" banner created a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, and regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom. The findings were presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at the report's launch.

Bartın stands under the national framework described for Turkey. That framework records police stops of trans women for background checks, in which foreign visitors must produce original identity documents; a passport-carrying duty for foreigners with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira; trans prisoners placed according to registered sex; and a Health Ministry tightening of transition-related care records. Provincial police and health boards administer these same instruments in Bartın, so any document check, medical request or public-space encounter carries the outing risk identified nationally.
tangentialFactors:
The 11th Judicial Package reaches beyond trans people. Its ceremony provision would criminalise participation in same-sex engagements and marriages, so the draft's impact on visitors and residents is not confined to gender identity, and the coalition opposing it includes LGB as well as trans-focused organisations.

Enforcement concentrations reported in Turkey's largest city reflect where stops occur rather than where the legal basis exists. The provisions under which trans women were stopped and documented rest on national law, which means a quieter province offers no different legal ground, only lower encounter frequency.

Kaos GL records restrictions on freedom of expression and artistic freedom by regulatory and supervisory bodies as part of the same policy wave. Public cultural and Pride-type events are therefore subject to administrative pressure alongside street-level policing.

Organised opposition is documented. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association have taken positions against the draft package, and Kaos GL's report was launched through public advocacy by lawyer Kerem Dikmen, indicating functioning domestic rights infrastructure even under the documented restrictions.
localsOnly:
Residents seeking gender-affirming care face the draft package's proposed rise in the minimum age from 18 to 25 and its proposed permanent-infertility condition, with treating physicians exposed to punishment. Whether any of these conditions already reaches patients through administrative circulars rather than enacted statute is not established in the sources.

Participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony would become a criminal offence carrying up to four years' imprisonment under the draft, a provision that would bind residents regardless of their own gender history.

Domestic organising and public speech are constrained by instructions issued to public institutions under the "Year of the Family" banner and by regulatory and supervisory bodies restricting expression and artistic freedom. Kaos GL frames this as hostility converted into institutional policy, with senior officials' hate speech setting the tone for public administration.

Residents accused under "general morality" and "biological sex" provisions would enter a penal system that holds trans prisoners according to registered sex and, per the national record, manages LGBT detainees through segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement.
outOfScopeNotes:
The legislative status of the 11th Judicial Package is unresolved in these sources. Human Rights Watch reports it as a leaked draft before the government; whether it has since been enacted, amended or withdrawn is not sourced here.

Whether Bartın's police, health directorates or courts have applied any of the instruments described is not sourced. The record contains no province-level enforcement data, no recorded stops, charges or denials of care attributable to Bartın.

Whether the proposed age-25 and infertility conditions operate in any area through existing administrative circulars, rather than only as pending legislation, is not established by the inventory and remains open.

The Kaos GL findings are presented as national aggregates with no provincial breakdown, so the distribution of the reported institutional instructions across provinces is not resolvable from this record.
